events.before: Home Newsroom JLC Global launches CNC Machining Service JLC Global launches CNC Machining Service Product Update Aug 16, 2024 Table of Contents What Make JLC Global' CNC Machining Service Different? Quality & Delivery In Conclusion We're proud to announce that our CNC Machining service officially launched in July of this year. Thank s to t he trust and support of all of you. W e've seamlessly transitioned from a trial run to a fully operational service and gained recognition from an ever-growing customer base in just three months with the fine-tuned process. What Make JLC Global ' CNC Machining Service Different? We offer a wide spectrum of machining services with cutting-edge technology. Our impressive array of processing equipment includes 3-axis and 5-axis machining centers, 3+2 machining, lathes, milling-turning combinations, wire cutting, electrical discharge machining, surface grinding, gear hobbing machines, tapping machines, ultrasonic cleaning machines, sandblasting machines, deburring machines, and laser marking machines. Not limited to metal alloys such as aluminum (6061, 7075) and copper (brass, bronze), we are also proficient in working with plastic materials like ABS, engineering plastics, electric wood, and acrylic. What sets us apart is our comprehensive offering of surface treatments, including sandblasting, brushing, anodizing, laser marking and etc. Quality & Delivery Quality and on-time delivery have always been our top priorities. To ensure the highest quality standards, we've invested in state-of-the-art inspection equipment such as two-dimensional and 3D scanning measurement devices, flash testers, spectral analyzers, tool wear detection equipment, height gauges, a complete set of gauges, thread gauges, micrometers and etc. Our experienced quality engineers oversee structural component inspections, guaranteeing reliable product and services for you. . While our CNC business currently focuses on prototyping and small batches, we're committed to serving a broader customer base. On average, our prototype orders have a lead time of approximately 5 days, with the possibility of expedited production in as fast as 3 days. We're continuously optimizing our processes to provide even more efficient services. In Conclusion Thank you for being an integral part of our journey to success! Your support means the world to JLC Global ! We will try our best in continuing to provide the best services to all of you! Keep Joining us in this incredible journey towards CNC machining. Get free quote now! Table of Contents What Make JLC Global' CNC Machining Service Different? Quality & Delivery In Conclusion

events.before: Home Newsroom Important Notice: Logistics Policy Updates due to the US’s tariff on China Important Notice: Logistics Policy Updates due to the US’s tariff on China Price Update Apr 23, 2025 Table of Contents US Tariff Timeline: New options available: Notes: US Tariff Timeline: February 4, 2025: U.S. President Donald Trump imposed 10% tariffs on all Chinese imports March 3, 2025: The US levied an additional 10% tariff on China, leading to a total of 20% tariffs April 5, 2025: The US's 10% reciprocal tariff went into effect and will impose 34% reciprocal tariffs on April 9 April 9, 2025: The US increased the reciprocal tariffs from 34% to 84% April 10, 2025: The US again raised the reciprocal tariffs on Chinese goods to 125% Taking into account the additional tariff and reciprocal tariffs, the total amounts to 145% . Due to the fluctuating customs duty rate (145%~175%), we will collect taxes from customers in advance based on the highest rate of 175%. After receiving the tax bill from the logistics provider, any excess will be refunded, and any shortfall will be charged accordingly. See more details here: https://jlccnc.com/help/article/us-tariff-policy-faq The following adjustments have been made: Effective from 20:20 on April 22nd(GMT+8), B2C customers placing orders destined for the United States are required to choose DDP when selecting the shipping method and prepay 175% of the order value as taxes. New options available: · DHL Express Priority (DDP) · FedEx International Priority (DDP) · UPS Express Saver (DDP) Notes: 1. All tax charges can be adjusted after actual tax bills are issued by the carriers. Any excess will be refunded, and any shortfall will be charged accordingly. 2. DHL Express and FedEx Express options are now restricted to corporate customers only. 3. YunExpress small packet options and self-use DHL, FedEx account(Non-DDP) remain unaffected. If you have any questions about the above information or need order support, please contact our customer service team support@jlcpcb.com . events.before: Home Newsroom JLCCNC Now Supports Merged Ordering with JLCMC JLCCNC Now Supports Merged Ordering with JLCMC Product Update Dec 18, 2025 Table of Contents Three Reasons to Merge Your Orders How to Place a Merged Order Better Supporting Manufacturing Needs Through Stronger Platform Collaboration Media Contact: JLCCNC is thrilled to announce a significant upgrade to its ordering experience. Starting December 13, merged ordering capabilities have been further expanded across the JLCMC mechanical ecosystem. Previously, merged ordering was already available for services such as 3D printing and sheet metal fabrication. With this update, JLCCNC orders can now be combined with JLCMC products in the same checkout, with consolidated shipping and a unified batch number. Three Reasons to Merge Your Orders 1. One Workflow for Everything By adding products from different business lines to one cart, you reduce administrative overhead and eliminate the need to track multiple payment requests. 2. Reduced Logistics Costs Consolidated shipping allows you to bundle those diverse items into one package. This reduces the number of base-weight charges you pay and simplifies receiving logistics. 3. Unified Order Management Managing multiple order numbers increases the risk of error. You will receive a unified batch number for all your items, making tracking more intuitive and ensuring all parts of your project arrive together. How to Place a Merged Order 1. Add your CNC machining parts, along with other items such as JLCMC products, to your shopping cart. 2. Go to the Shopping Cart page and select the “All” checkbox to group your items from different platforms. 3. Confirm the merged order and the system will automatically generate a unified batch number and calculate a single shipping rate for the merged order. events.before: Home Newsroom JLCCNC CNC Prototyping Subsidy: Parts from $2 JLCCNC CNC Prototyping Subsidy: Parts from $2 Events Nov 09, 2026 Table of Contents CNC Prototype Parts Starting at $2 Manufacturing Standards for Promotional Parts How to Apply for the CNC Prototyping Subsidy JLCCNC is offering special pricing on CNC-machined prototypes for hardware developers and product designers. Customers can receive special pricing on up to 10 CNC prototype parts per month , with prices ranging from $2 to $7 per part . The offer is designed for functional metal prototypes, giving developers a more affordable way to test their designs before placing a standard CNC order. Pricing depends on the part's dimensions and the machining work required. CNC Prototype Parts Starting at $2 The promotion covers Aluminum 6061 parts within the following dimensional limits: Without side features: From 2×2×2mm to 200×200×15mm. Length and width cannot both be below 10mm. With side features: From 25×5×6mm to 100×90×55mm. Side holes and pockets are supported, along with slots. The system can also automatically detect threaded holes through DFM analysis. The final promotional price depends on the part design and its machining requirements. Manufacturing Standards for Promotional Parts Promotional parts use Aluminum 6061 as the default material, with bead blasting and anodizing as the standard surface finish. JLCCNC machines these parts to ISO 2768-m (Medium) tolerances. Automatic thread recognition is supported, and a default C0.2 mm chamfer at 45° is applied to edges. The promotion is intended for functional prototypes rather than high-end cosmetic parts. Minor surface blemishes are not covered by the promotional claim policy. This exclusion also applies to slight anodizing shade variations and rack contact marks. Customers who need Class-A cosmetic surfaces should place a standard CNC machining order. How to Apply for the CNC Prototyping Subsidy To participate, upload a 3D CAD model in STEP or STP format through the Monthly CNC Prototyping Subsidy page . Files can be up to 100 MB. Each uploaded model first goes through an automated AI DFM check. JLCCNC's engineering team then reviews the design manually before production. Parts that do not pass manual verification will not qualify for the promotion. Each customer can receive special pricing on up to 10 parts per month. Daily promotional slots depend on factory capacity and are allocated on a first-come, first-served basis. Each customer is limited to one account under the fair-use policy. The subsidy program is ongoing. For complete eligibility requirements and CAD preparation instructions, visit the special deal design guidelines before uploading a model. CNC Prototypes from $2 Special pricing on up to 10 Aluminum 6061 prototype parts per month. events.before: Home Newsroom JLCCNC Service Update: Price Adjustment for CNC Machining Services JLCCNC Service Update: Price Adjustment for CNC Machining Services Price Update May 08, 2026 Table of Contents Core Reasons for Adjustment Implementation Details Our Commitment to Your Success [May 8, 2026] – To our valued customers and partners, Thank you for your continued trust in JLCCNC. We are dedicated to providing the high-precision, stable, and reliable CNC manufacturing services your projects demand. Following a comprehensive evaluation of current market conditions, JLCCNC will implement a price adjustment for our CNC machining services, effective May 8, 2026 (18:00 UTC+8) . This decision is driven by sustained and significant cost increases in core raw materials and manufacturing consumables. Core Reasons for Adjustment ● Surge in Tooling Costs: The price of Tungsten Powder—the primary raw material for high-performance CNC cutting tools—has surged by 491% year-over-year. This unprecedented spike has drastically increased our operational consumables cost. ● Rising Raw Material Prices: The market price of Aluminum, our most frequently utilized processing material, has risen by 20%, leading to higher procurement expenses across our supply chain. Implementation Details ● Effective Date: May 8, 2026 (18:00 UTC+8). ● Instant Quote System: Updated pricing will be reflected automatically in the [JLCCNC Online Instant Quote System] . ● Market-Linked Flexibility: JLCCNC maintains a dynamic pricing model. Should the market prices of Tungsten or Aluminum decrease, we will adjust and lower our processing fees accordingly at the earliest opportunity. Note: Due to ongoing market volatility, future pricing updates may be applied directly to our online system without separate formal announcements. Our Commitment to Your Success We recognize that pricing changes impact your project planning. This adjustment is essential to ensure we do not compromise on the quality and delivery stability you expect from JLCCNC. We remain committed to your success through: ● Strict Quality Assurance: Maintaining rigorous inspection standards for every part. ● Global Competitiveness: Ensuring our pricing remains highly competitive compared to international benchmarks, without sacrificing quality. ● Expert Technical Support: Our engineering team remains available 24/7 for material selection and process optimization to help you mitigate costs. We sincerely appreciate your understanding of this market-driven decision. We look forward to our continued partnership and to delivering the exceptional manufacturing solutions your business deserves. Full Range of Surface Finishes Quality & Fast Delivery In Conclusion About JLCCNC Media Contact: We are thrilled to announce that JLCCNC's Sheet Metal Fabrication Service has officially launched after a successful one-month trial run! Thanks to the trust and support of our valued customers, we have smoothly transitioned from trial operation to full-scale production . Within just a month, our sheet metal service has gained recognition for its high precision, versatile material options, and refined surface finishing capabilities . What Makes JLCCNC Sheet Metal Fabrication Different? At JLCCNC, we combine precision, efficiency, and flexibility to deliver high-quality sheet metal parts — from prototypes to small-batch production. Our advanced sheet metal production line features CNC laser cutting machines, bending machines, punching machines, and welding stations , enabling us to process complex geometries with tight tolerances. We specialize in working with the following materials: Aluminum 5052 Stainless Steel 201 Stainless Steel 304 Cold Rolled Steel Galvanized Steel Sheet Whether it's structural enclosures, electronic housings, or custom brackets, our team ensures excellent fit, finish, and durability for every part. Full Range of Surface Finishes To meet both aesthetic and functional requirements, JLCCNC offers a comprehensive suite of surface treatments , including: Anodizing Hardcoat Anodizing Conductive Anodizing Powder Coating Brushing Silkscreen Printing Laser Marking With our online quoting system , you can preview each surface finish and get an instant quote — simply upload your file, select the finish, and receive your quote immediately . Minimum order price starts from $0.4 , making it flexible for all project sizes. Quality & Fast Delivery Just like our CNC services, quality and rapid delivery are our top priorities. Our inspection team uses precision measuring instruments, including 2D projectors, thickness gauges, and surface testers , to ensure every part meets strict standards before shipment. The fastest production cycle can be completed in just one day , providing you with highly efficient and convenient sheet metal services. In Conclusion The official launch of JLCCNC Sheet Metal Fabrication Service marks another milestone in our mission to deliver comprehensive, one-stop manufacturing solutions . Overview of U.S. Tariff Policies on Imports from China 2.What is the rate of JLCCNC's advance tax collection? New Tariff Policy Current Tariff Composition: Updated Tariff Prepayment Plan About Tariff Refunds Special Circumstances US Tariff Timeline: New options available: Notes: This page contains consolidated and continuously updated information regarding changes to JLCPCB, JLCMC, JLCCNC, and JLC3DP's logistics and tax policies affected by the U.S. tariff on China. Please check back regularly for the latest updates. Latest Update: Updated on March 17 , 2026 Effective February 24, 2026, the Reciprocal Tariffs and Fentanyl-related Tariffs have expired. Concurrently, a new 10% provisional tariff has been implemented. In response to these changes,we will adjust the US DDP tariff rates starting March 17, 2026 , resulting in an overall reduction of 10%. Please refer to the table below for details: Type Material Rate PCB / 35.00% SMT / 35.00% Stencil / 90.00% 3D Resin、Nylon、PA12-CF、ABS、ASA、PLA、TPU Plastic 40.00% 3D 316L、BJ-316L 70.00% 3D Titanium TC4 35.00% CNC ABS、POM、Bakelite、PMMA、FR4、Nylon、Polycarbonate 40.00% CNC SUS304 70.00% CNC Aluminum 6061、Aluminum 7075 90.00% CNC Copper - T2 90.00% CNC Brass - H59 90.00% CNC 45# Steel 80.00% FA / 55.00% Sheet Metal Aluminum 90.00% Sheet Metal Stainless Steel 70.00% Sheet Metal Steel Alloy 70.00% Flexible Heater / 35.00% Updated on November 11 , 2025 We will determine the advance tax collection rate based on the product's type and material. Starting November 11, 2025, the additional tariff rate will be reduced from 20% to 10%, along with an overall 10% reduction in prepaid tariffs. Updated on August 12, 2025 On August 11, 2025, the U.S. government issued a joint statement confirming the continued enforcement of Executive Order No. 14257, as amended on May 14. The reciprocal tariff rate will remain at 10% (part of a total 34% rate, with the remaining 24% suspended for an additional 90 days and potentially raised to the full 34% thereafter). JLCCNC's tariff policy for exports to the United States remains unchanged. Updated on June 12, 2025 1. Overview of U.S. Tariff Policies on Imports from China On May 14, 2025, the U.S. government adjusted the tariff rates on Chinese imports, resulting in a general reduction for certain categories of goods. Additional Tariffs: 20% Reciprocal Tariffs: 125% 10% (for 90 days, may be raised to 34% in the future) Section 301 Tariffs: 25% Section 232 Tariffs: 25% 50%(raised on June 4th 2025, the tariff only apply to steel products and aluminum alloy products.) Verify Now Blog > 12 PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Component Placement 12 PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Component Placement by: Mila Oct 29,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB Layout PCB Component Placement PCB Layout Guidelines PCB Design Guidelines PCB layout involves more than simply placing components and routing traces. Component spacing, decoupling capacitor placement, pad connections, thermal management, and manufacturing constraints all affect PCB assembly quality and long-term reliability. The following PCB layout guidelines cover 12 practical details that engineers should consider during PCB component placement and design. 1. SMT Component Spacing The spacing between surface-mount technology (SMT) components is an important consideration in PCB layout. Insufficient spacing can make solder paste printing and component placement more difficult, increase the risk of solder bridging, and complicate rework and maintenance. The following values can serve as preliminary references for PCB component spacing: Same-type components: A spacing of at least 0.3 mm may be used as a reference. Different types of components: A spacing of at least 0.13 × h + 0.3 mm may be used as a reference, where h is the maximum height difference between adjacent components. Components requiring manual placement or rework: A spacing of at least 1.5 mm may be considered, depending on the available working space and tools. These values are for reference only and are not universal manufacturing standards. Actual PCB component spacing should be determined based on component packages, pad dimensions, solder paste printing, placement equipment, and the manufacturing and assembly capabilities of the PCB supplier. 2. Spacing Between Through-Hole and SMT Components Adequate spacing should also be maintained between through-hole components and SMT components to prevent interference during component placement, soldering, and subsequent rework. A spacing of 1–3 mm can serve as a general reference, but the actual distance depends on component dimensions, lead positions, soldering methods, and maintenance requirements. For PCBs assembled using wave soldering, engineers should also consider component orientation, shadowing effects caused by adjacent components, and whether solder can reach the joints effectively. 3. IC Decoupling Capacitor Placement Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as practical to the corresponding IC power pins. This helps shorten the current loop between the power supply and ground, reducing parasitic inductance and power supply noise. When an IC has multiple power pins, the number, capacitance, and placement of decoupling capacitors should be determined according to the datasheet, power distribution network, and actual current requirements. Where individual power pins require dedicated decoupling, the corresponding capacitors should be placed as close to those pins as possible. The grounding path is equally important. Keep the connections between the power pin, decoupling capacitor, and ground as short as practical. Unnecessarily long traces or excessive vias can reduce decoupling effectiveness, particularly at high frequencies. 4. Component Orientation and Clearance Near PCB Edges PCBs often undergo routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes. Components near PCB edges therefore require special attention to their orientation and clearance. First, consider the mechanical stress generated during depanelization. Ceramic capacitors, connectors, and other mechanically sensitive components should be positioned to minimize stress concentration at solder joints and component bodies. Component orientation should be determined by the depanelization method, pad geometry, and component characteristics rather than by a universal rule that all components must be parallel to the cutting direction. Second, sufficient component-free space should be maintained near PCB edges to prevent damage from cutting tools or depanelization equipment. The required clearance depends on the depanelization method, such as V-scoring, routing, or mouse bites, as well as component dimensions and the PCB manufacturer's capabilities. For components that are particularly sensitive to mechanical stress, consider using a depanelization method that reduces stress on the board and solder joints. 5. Connecting Adjacent PCB Pads When adjacent pads must be connected to the same net, the copper connections and trace widths should be planned carefully. Poorly designed copper connections may reduce the effective clearance between pads and increase the risk of solder bridging. During PCB layout, maintain adequate electrical clearance between pads and select trace widths according to current-carrying requirements. For fine-pitch components, pay particular attention to the relationship between pads, traces, and solder mask openings to avoid problems with solder paste printing and soldering quality. After completing the layout, run design rule checks (DRC) and verify that the design meets the PCB manufacturer's fabrication and assembly requirements. 6. Thermal Relief vs. Solid Copper Connections When a pad is connected to a copper plane, the connection method should be selected based on soldering requirements, current-carrying capacity, and thermal performance. Two common methods are thermal relief connections and solid copper connections. A thermal relief connection uses several narrow copper spokes to connect the pad to the surrounding copper plane. This reduces heat transfer from the pad into the larger copper area during soldering, making soldering and rework easier in many cases. A solid copper connection directly connects the pad to the copper plane. It generally provides lower electrical and thermal resistance, but the larger copper area can draw heat away from the pad, making it more difficult to reach the required soldering temperature. The appropriate method depends on current requirements, heat dissipation, soldering processes, and rework needs. For high-current or thermally demanding connections, do not reduce the number or width of copper spokes solely to make soldering easier without evaluating the electrical and thermal consequences. 7. Using Teardrops in PCB Layout When a trace connects to a pad or via through a narrow junction, a teardrop can be added where appropriate to create a smoother transition between the trace and the connection point. Teardrops offer several potential benefits: Improved connection reliability: They increase the copper area at the trace-to-pad junction, helping reduce the risk of a weakened or broken connection caused by drill misalignment, manufacturing tolerances, or mechanical stress. Enhanced mechanical robustness: The wider transition can make the connection less vulnerable to local narrowing or separation. Improved appearance: Teardrops create a smoother visual transition between traces and pads. However, teardrops are not necessary in every situation. For high-speed or impedance-sensitive traces, engineers should evaluate whether the resulting geometric changes could affect impedance continuity or signal integrity. 8. Trace Width at Component Pads During PCB layout, trace widths near component pads should be selected according to the electrical and mechanical requirements of the design. For differential signals, symmetrical analog circuits, and connections requiring balanced current distribution, trace symmetry, width matching, and length matching may be important for maintaining signal integrity and circuit performance. However, ordinary signal traces do not always need to have identical widths on both sides of a pad. Trace widths should be determined by current-carrying capacity, impedance requirements, pad dimensions, and manufacturing capabilities. Avoid unnecessary abrupt changes in trace width near pad connections. 9. Handling Unused IC Pins Unused IC pins must be handled according to the device datasheet and application requirements. They should not all be connected to ground or left floating indiscriminately. For example: NC pins: Follow the datasheet instructions. Some pins must remain unconnected and should not be grounded without authorization. Unused input pins: Connect them to the specified logic level or use the recommended pull-up, pull-down, or other biasing method to prevent undefined input states. Unused output pins: Do not connect them directly to ground or a power rail unless the datasheet explicitly permits it. Pins permitted to float: Leave them unconnected only when this is allowed or required by the device documentation. For physical pins that are present on the IC but not used in the application, ensure that the PCB footprint correctly represents the actual package. Whether the corresponding pads should be connected to ground or handled in another way depends on the pin function and the device manufacturer's recommendations. Adding a pad and connecting it to ground does not necessarily provide effective shielding. An incorrect connection may instead cause a short circuit or interfere with normal device operation. 10. Via-in-Pad Design Considerations During PCB layout, placing a conventional open via directly within a pad can cause solder to flow into the hole during assembly. This may result in insufficient solder at the joint, poor soldering quality, or other assembly defects. For ordinary SMT pads, avoid placing untreated open vias directly within the pads, particularly for fine-pitch components, unless the manufacturing process supports the design. However, vias are not universally prohibited within pads. Via-in-pad is a common design approach for packages such as BGAs, where routing density and electrical performance may require it. Depending on the application, via filling, capping, or other appropriate via treatments may be needed to prevent solder loss and ensure reliable assembly. Select the appropriate approach based on the component package, via structure, and PCB manufacturer's process capabilities. 11. PCB Edge Clearance for Traces, Pads, and Components Copper traces, pads, and components should maintain adequate clearance from PCB edges to prevent damage during fabrication, depanelization, and subsequent assembly. If copper features or pads are too close to the board edge, routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes may damage the copper, expose conductors, or compromise electrical reliability. For single-sided boards and substrates with relatively low mechanical strength, additional attention should be paid to structural integrity and component placement near the edges. The required PCB edge clearance should be determined according to the board material, thickness, depanelization method, and manufacturer's capabilities. Include these clearances in the PCB design rules and verify them before manufacturing. 12. Keep Electrolytic Capacitors Away from Heat Sources Electrolytic capacitors are sensitive to operating temperature. Prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures can accelerate electrolyte loss and shorten capacitor service life. During PCB layout, avoid placing electrolytic capacitors too close to power resistors, power semiconductors, transformers, or other heat-generating components whenever possible. If close placement is unavoidable, evaluate the thermal impact based on component temperature rise, airflow direction, and the actual operating environment. Also consider the capacitor's rated operating temperature, ripple current, and self-heating to ensure that it operates within acceptable limits under real-world conditions. Distance from a heat source alone is not sufficient to determine whether a capacitor is safe. Thermal design and the operating conditions of the complete product must also be considered. Conclusion PCB layout affects not only electrical performance but also manufacturability, soldering quality, and long-term reliability. In addition to routing and component placement, engineers should consider assembly processes, mechanical stress, thermal requirements, and the recommendations provided in component datasheets. After completing the PCB design, perform design rule checks and verify the layout against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities and assembly requirements. Careful attention to these PCB layout guidelines can help reduce design issues and improve PCB fabrication and assembly reliability Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Clock Circuit Design Guidelines for PCB Layout Clock Circuit Design Guidelines for PCB Layout by: Mila Nov 06,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout clock circuit crystal oscillator pcb Layout pcb clock signal routing Clock circuits play an essential role in electronic systems by providing timing signals that synchronize the operation of different components. However, improper clock circuit design can lead to signal interference, timing errors, and system instability. This article explores the PCB design guidelines for crystal circuits, active oscillators, and clock distributors, covering key considerations for component placement, signal routing, and noise reduction. 1. Crystal A clock is an essential part of any electronic system. It acts like the heartbeat of the system, providing synchronization signals to different components. If the clock signal becomes unstable or fails, the entire system may malfunction or stop working. Therefore, proper clock circuit design is essential in PCB design. Common clock sources and distribution components used in PCBs include crystals, oscillators, and clock distributors. Some ICs may generate their own clock signals internally. However, the clock signal ultimately originates from a crystal, an oscillator, or another clock source before being distributed to other components. When designing a crystal circuit, consider the following guidelines: Place the crystal as close as possible to the IC's oscillator pins to minimize trace length and reduce external interference. For designs with high electromagnetic compatibility requirements, consider using a crystal with a metal shield package. Ensure that the shield is properly grounded according to the component datasheet. Avoid routing other signal traces beneath the crystal and its load capacitors, especially high-speed digital signals. A continuous GND reference plane can be provided beneath the crystal circuit according to the IC manufacturer's layout recommendations. Keep high-speed digital signal traces away from the crystal to reduce crosstalk. Keep the ground connections of the load capacitors as short as possible to minimize parasitic inductance and provide a low-impedance return path. A GND guard area can be added around the crystal according to the recommended layout. If necessary, use GND vias to connect the ground copper on different layers. Place the crystal and its two load capacitors close to the IC's oscillator pins. Follow the component manufacturer's reference design for the exact placement arrangement. Common crystal packages used in PCB design include 2-pin through-hole packages, 2-pin SMD packages, and 4-pin SMD packages. （Common crystal package types） Although crystals are available in different package sizes and specifications, their basic operating principles and peripheral circuit designs are similar. Therefore, many PCB placement and routing guidelines are applicable across different crystal designs. A basic crystal circuit is shown below: （Basic crystal circuit schematic） The two capacitors shown in the schematic are load capacitors. They connect the two crystal terminals to ground and provide the required load capacitance for stable oscillation. Their values should be determined based on the crystal datasheet, the IC's internal oscillator characteristics, and the parasitic capacitance of the PCB. 2. Crystal Circuit Placement and Routing When placing a crystal circuit, position the two load capacitors as close as possible to the crystal and the IC's oscillator pins. This helps minimize trace length and reduce the impact of parasitic parameters. The placement is shown below: （Crystal circuit placement） When routing the crystal circuit, keep the two connections between the crystal and the IC as short as possible and preferably close to each other to reduce parasitic capacitance and external interference. Note that these two traces are not true differential signal lines, so differential routing rules should not be applied directly. Avoid unnecessary vias and follow the IC manufacturer's layout recommendations to determine whether GND guard traces are needed. The routing layout is shown below: （Crystal circuit routing） 3. Crystal Circuit Design Variations The circuit described above is the most basic and commonly used crystal circuit design. In practical PCB designs, additional components such as series resistors and test points may be included to meet debugging or signal integrity requirements. However, the basic design principles remain the same. Based on the guidelines above, consider the following points when placing components: （Crystal circuit layout with a series resistor and test point） Place the crystal, associated capacitors, and series resistor on the same PCB layer whenever possible to reduce vias and shorten connection paths. If test points are required, avoid long stubs. Additional trace branches may introduce parasitic capacitance and affect oscillator stability. Avoid placing high-power components near the crystal, such as power ICs, MOSFETs, and inductors, as heat generated by these components may affect crystal frequency stability. Routing guidelines: Place and route the crystal on the same layer as the IC whenever possible to minimize vias. If layer changes are necessary, ensure a continuous return path and add nearby GND vias when needed. Keep crystal traces as short as possible. Trace width should be determined based on the IC manufacturer's recommendations and PCB fabrication capabilities rather than increased unnecessarily. GND guard traces can be added around the crystal circuit when appropriate. Connect them to the reference ground plane using GND vias. Keep the crystal circuit area relatively isolated. Avoid routing other high-speed signals through this area to reduce crosstalk and external noise interference. 4. Oscillator Circuit Design Unlike passive crystals, active oscillators integrate an internal oscillation circuit and can directly output clock signals. An active oscillator circuit typically consists of an oscillator device, a power supply decoupling circuit, and an optional source-series resistor selected according to the output interface and load requirements. A typical oscillator circuit is shown below: （Active oscillator circuit schematic） The PCB placement and routing layout is shown below: （Active oscillator PCB layout and routing） Placement and routing guidelines: Place power decoupling capacitors as close as possible to the oscillator's power supply pins. Prioritize a short power and ground loop for the high-frequency decoupling capacitor. If multiple decoupling capacitors are used, select their capacitance values and placement based on the component datasheet and power integrity requirements. There is no need to mechanically follow a fixed large-to-small capacitor arrangement. Determine whether a source-series resistor is needed based on the oscillator's output type, drive capability, trace length, and load conditions. If required, place it as close as possible to the oscillator output pin. Determine the clock signal impedance based on the oscillator output interface, receiver requirements, and PCB stackup. For clock signals that require transmission line control, implement appropriate impedance design. For long clock traces, consider routing them on an inner layer while maintaining a continuous reference plane. If layer transitions are necessary, add nearby GND return vias when appropriate. Maintain adequate spacing between clock traces and other signal traces to reduce crosstalk. The required spacing depends on signal edge rate, trace length, and layer-to-layer coupling. For designs with high electromagnetic compatibility requirements, consider using a crystal with a metal shield package. Ensure that the shield is properly grounded according to the component datasheet. Avoid routing other signal traces beneath the crystal and its load capacitors, especially high-speed digital signals. A continuous GND reference plane can be provided beneath the crystal circuit according to the IC manufacturer's layout recommendations. Keep high-speed digital signal traces away from the crystal to reduce crosstalk. Keep the ground connections of the load capacitors as short as possible to minimize parasitic inductance and provide a low-impedance return path. Verify Now Blog > Differential Pair Routing: 3 Common Design Mistakes to Avoid Differential Pair Routing: 3 Common Design Mistakes to Avoid by: Mila Nov 04,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout Differential Pair Differential Pair Routing High-Speed PCB Design Differential Pair Routing In high-speed PCB design , differential pairs are increasingly used, especially in high-speed interfaces such as USB, HDMI, and PCIe. These interfaces commonly use differential signaling for reliable data transmission. Why is differential signaling so widely used? Compared with conventional single-ended routing, differential pairs offer better noise immunity, help suppress common-mode noise and electromagnetic interference (EMI), and improve signal integrity and timing performance. Differential Pair Routing Requirements In PCB design, a differential pair consists of two closely coupled signal traces. To ensure signal transmission quality, these traces generally need to have matched lengths, equal widths, consistent spacing, and symmetrical routing. Differential impedance must also be controlled according to the design requirements. （Differential Pair Routing Requirements） 1. Equal Length Equal length means keeping the two traces in a differential pair as close in length as possible. The purpose is to control the propagation delay difference (skew) between the two signals, maintain proper timing alignment, and reduce signal imbalance and the resulting common-mode noise. 2. Equal Width and Spacing Equal width means maintaining the same trace width for both signals. Equal spacing means keeping the distance between the two traces as consistent as possible, allowing them to run symmetrically and in parallel. This helps maintain a stable coupling relationship between the two traces, minimizes differential impedance variations, and improves signal transmission quality. 3. Controlled Differential Impedance When designing a PCB with differential pairs, one of the first steps is to determine the target differential impedance required by the interface and plan the routing accordingly. It is also important to minimize impedance variations along the routing path. Differential impedance is affected by several factors, including trace width, spacing between the two traces, copper thickness, PCB material, and stackup structure. These factors should all be considered during the design process to maintain consistent differential impedance. 4. Maintain a Continuous Reference Plane Although differential signals offer strong noise immunity, they still require an appropriate reference plane. The reference plane beneath the differential pair should remain continuous whenever possible. Avoid routing differential pairs across split ground planes or slots in the reference plane, as these discontinuities can alter return paths and cause impedance variations. Common Misconceptions About Differential Pair Routing Misconception 1: Differential Signals Do Not Need a Ground Plane as a Return Path, or the Two Traces Can Serve as Each Other's Return Paths. Differential signals offer strong immunity to common-mode noise, but this does not mean they do not need a reference plane. In fact, the return-current path depends on the coupling between the two differential traces and their coupling to the reference plane. Differential-mode return current is primarily associated with the electromagnetic coupling between the two traces, while the reference plane still affects the return path and impedance characteristics, especially for common-mode currents. When the reference plane contains splits or slots, the return-current path may change, causing impedance discontinuities, signal degradation, and increased EMI. Therefore, differential pairs should be routed over a continuous reference plane whenever possible, avoiding split ground regions. In addition, removing the reference plane beneath differential traces to suppress common-mode noise is not recommended. This can make impedance control more difficult and disrupt the return path for common-mode currents, potentially increasing electromagnetic radiation. （Differential Signal Reference Plane） Misconception 2: Maintaining Consistent Spacing Is More Important Than Matching Trace Lengths. In practical PCB routing, it is not always possible to satisfy every differential pair design requirement simultaneously. Component pin placement, via locations, and available routing space may require designers to introduce serpentine routing to match trace lengths. However, this can cause some sections of the differential pair to lose their parallel alignment or consistent spacing. In such cases, design priorities should be determined according to the interface specifications and application requirements. For high-speed differential interfaces with strict intra-pair skew limits, length matching is particularly important. However, trace spacing also affects coupling and differential impedance, so it should not be overlooked. During routing, priority should be given to meeting interface timing and impedance requirements. Symmetry, consistent spacing, and routing continuity should then be maintained as much as possible, rather than focusing on just one routing parameter. （Differential Line Length Matching） Misconception 3: Differential Traces Must Always Be Routed Close Together. Routing differential traces close together strengthens the coupling between them, improving noise immunity and helping reduce electromagnetic radiation through partial magnetic field cancellation. However, closer spacing is not always better. The spacing should be determined by the target differential impedance, PCB stackup, and application requirements. Excessively small spacing may make impedance control and manufacturing more challenging. To reduce crosstalk, maintain sufficient spacing between differential pairs and other signal traces. The 4W rule (spacing of at least four times the trace width) can serve as an initial guideline, but actual spacing should be determined by the design requirements. Ground guard traces connected to the reference plane through stitching vias can also provide additional isolation. For high-frequency applications, coplanar waveguide (CPW) structures are another option for controlling differential impedance. （Differential Line Spacing） Conclusion Differential pair routing is an important part of high-speed PCB design . In addition to trace length, width, and spacing, designers must also consider differential impedance, reference-plane continuity, and interference from surrounding signals. Only by considering all these factors together can designers ensure reliable differential signal transmission and improve overall PCB performance and reliability. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Considerations for Single-Point and Multi-Point Grounding PCB Layout Considerations for Single-Point and Multi-Point Grounding by: Mila Oct 27,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB Layout single point grounding Single-Point and Multi-Point Grounding PCB grounding is an important part of PCB layout , affecting circuit stability, noise levels, signal integrity, and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC). Different circuits have different grounding requirements, and single-point grounding, multi-point grounding, and mixed grounding each have their own applications. This article explains the differences between these grounding techniques and highlights key considerations for effective PCB grounding. 1. Basic Principles of PCB Grounding In a PCB, ground provides a voltage reference for the circuit and a return path for current. Ideally, the ground plane should have low impedance. However, copper traces, vias, and connection structures introduce parasitic resistance and inductance. As frequency increases, parasitic inductance generally has a greater impact on grounding impedance. Therefore, PCB grounding design should consider not only DC resistance but also signal frequency, return paths, and reference-plane continuity. Key considerations include: Minimize grounding impedance: Use ground planes, copper pours, and vias appropriately to reduce unnecessary impedance along grounding paths. Control noise coupling: Arrange sensitive analog circuits, digital circuits, and power circuits to minimize interference. Maintain continuous return paths: For high-speed signals, avoid reference-plane splits and other structures that force return currents to take detours. Choose an appropriate grounding technique: No single grounding method is suitable for every PCB layout. 2. Three Common PCB Grounding Techniques （Single-Point vs. Multi-Point Grounding in PCB Design） Single-Point Grounding Single-point grounding connects multiple circuit grounds at a designated point to help reduce common-impedance coupling between circuit sections. This technique is often used in low-frequency analog circuits, sensor circuits, and other applications where coupling through shared ground paths is a concern. Key design considerations include: Choose the connection point carefully: Avoid routing large return currents through ground paths shared with sensitive analog circuits. Keep grounding paths short: Minimize unnecessary detours while maintaining appropriate electrical connections. Consider high-frequency behavior: Single-point grounding is not always suitable for high-frequency circuits, as long grounding wires can introduce additional inductance. Multi-Point Grounding Multi-point grounding connects a circuit ground to a ground plane or grounding structure at multiple locations. This approach can shorten grounding paths and reduce impedance at high frequencies. It is commonly used in high-speed digital circuits, RF circuits, and designs that require low-impedance high-frequency return paths. Key design considerations include: Prioritize ground-plane continuity: Provide a stable reference path for signals, especially high-speed signals. Place ground vias appropriately: Add vias near connectors, shielding structures, and other locations where they help shorten return paths. Avoid unnecessary return-path detours: Check whether ground-plane slots, splits, or poorly planned connections could interrupt return currents. More ground vias do not automatically result in better grounding. Their placement and the overall return-path structure are equally important. Mixed Grounding Mixed grounding combines different grounding strategies according to the requirements of individual circuit sections. For example, a low-frequency sensitive analog circuit may use a designated single-point connection, while a high-speed digital circuit relies on a continuous ground plane and multiple grounding connections. This approach is useful for mixed-signal PCBs and complex systems with different frequency and current requirements. Key design considerations include: Separate circuit functions through layout: Arrange analog and digital components appropriately and route signals to reduce noise coupling. Evaluate ground separation carefully: Do not assume that all mixed-signal circuits require split ground planes. Plan return paths across circuit sections: If a split ground plane is necessary, ensure that signals crossing between sections have appropriate return paths. Comparison of PCB Grounding Techniques 3. PCB Grounding Guidelines for Single-Point and Multi-Point Grounding Single-Point Grounding Guidelines The main goal of single-point grounding is to control common impedance and prevent current from one circuit section from interfering with another through a shared grounding path. Plan ground connections carefully: Avoid routing large return currents through grounding paths shared with sensitive analog circuits. Minimize unnecessary path lengths: Reduce detours while maintaining appropriate circuit connections. Consider high-frequency performance: Do not select single-point grounding solely based on the number of circuit sections. Its suitability depends on the frequency range and circuit characteristics. Multi-Point Grounding Guidelines The main goal of multi-point grounding is to provide low-impedance, continuous return paths for current. Maintain ground-plane continuity: For high-speed signals, avoid routing across split reference-plane regions. Place ground vias strategically: Position vias near connectors, shielding structures, and other locations where they improve return-path continuity. The exact placement depends on the circuit and PCB structure. Minimize return-path detours: Check whether ground-plane slots, splits, or reference-layer changes could affect the return paths of critical signals. 4. Grounding Design for Mixed-Signal PCBs Mixed-signal PCBs contain both analog and digital circuits. Digital switching can generate transient currents, while analog circuits may be sensitive to small amounts of noise. The goal is to control noise coupling and provide appropriate return paths for different signals. Arrange Components into Functional Zones Arrange analog circuits, digital circuits, and switching power supplies according to their functions. Keep sensitive analog signal paths short and avoid routing high-speed digital signals through sensitive analog areas. For switching power supplies, pay particular attention to switching nodes and high-frequency current loops. Avoid placing these noisy areas close to sensitive analog circuits whenever possible. Handle AGND and DGND Carefully AGND and DGND refer to analog ground and digital ground, respectively. However, this does not mean that every PCB must separate them into two independent ground planes. For many mixed-signal circuits, a continuous ground plane combined with careful component placement, signal routing, and current-path management is a sensible starting point. If an IC datasheet specifies that AGND and DGND must be connected at a particular location, follow the manufacturer's recommendations. When using a 0-ohm resistor, ferrite bead, or another component to connect separate ground nets, evaluate its impedance and noise effects for the specific circuit rather than treating it as a universal solution. Maintain Continuous Signal Return Paths For high-speed signals, return current typically flows in the reference plane near the signal trace. If a trace crosses a ground-plane split, slot, or reference-layer transition, the return current may be forced to take a longer path. This can increase loop area and electromagnetic interference (EMI). Therefore, PCB layout should provide continuous reference planes for critical high-speed signals whenever possible. When a signal changes reference layers, verify that its return path remains adequately connected. （Mixed-Signal PCB Layout and Grounding Design） 5. Common PCB Grounding Mistakes and Solutions Conclusion There is no single grounding method that works for every PCB layout . Single-point grounding is suitable for some low-frequency sensitive circuits, multi-point grounding is often used where low-impedance high-frequency return paths are required, and mixed grounding combines strategies according to the needs of different circuit sections. In practical PCB layout, prioritize ground-plane continuity, current-loop design, common impedance, and signal return paths. Use IC datasheets, reference designs, and test results to guide design decisions. A well-planned grounding strategy can help reduce noise coupling, improve signal integrity, and enhance overall PCB stability. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production.
