Verify Now Blog > What Is the Purpose of a 1MΩ Resistor in a Crystal Oscillator Circuit What Is the Purpose of a 1MΩ Resistor in a Crystal Oscillator Circuit by: Mila Nov 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout crystal oscillator circuit crystal oscillator circuit design crystal oscillator pcb layout crystal oscillator design In crystal oscillator circuit design , you may notice that some circuits include a 1MΩ resistor connected in parallel with the crystal, while others do not. Why is this resistor used, and what happens if it is omitted? Although both configurations can work normally, the feedback resistor can play an important role in establishing the proper operating conditions for reliable crystal startup. Two Common Crystal Oscillator Circuit Configurations In actual product development, you may encounter two different configurations when designing a crystal oscillator circuit. In Figure 1, there is no 1MΩ resistor connected in parallel with the crystal, while Figure 2 shows a 1MΩ resistor connected across the crystal. Figure 1: Crystal oscillator circuit with a parallel 1MΩ resistor Figure 2: Crystal oscillator circuit without a parallel 1MΩ resistor Problem Description In some circuit designs, the system operates normally when a 1MΩ resistor is connected in parallel with the crystal. However, without this resistor, the program may start slowly, run abnormally, or even fail to start. Why Is a 1MΩ Resistor Used in a Crystal Oscillator Circuit? 1. How Does the 1MΩ Feedback Resistor Work? In a typical Pierce crystal oscillator circuit, the MCU's internal inverter acts as an amplifier. For the circuit to oscillate reliably, the inverter must operate within its linear region, where it can provide sufficient gain. The 1MΩ resistor connected in parallel with the crystal serves as a feedback resistor. It provides a DC feedback path and helps establish a suitable bias point for the inverter without significantly loading the oscillation signal. 2. Why Can Some Crystal Oscillators Work Without a 1MΩ Resistor? Not every crystal oscillator circuit requires an external 1MΩ feedback resistor. Some MCUs already integrate the necessary feedback or bias circuitry. In these designs, the internal circuit can establish the appropriate operating point without an additional external resistor. However, if the feedback path is insufficient, the inverter may not operate at the intended bias point. This can result in: Slow crystal startup. Unstable oscillation. Failure to start. 3. How Does Temperature Affect Crystal Oscillator Startup? Temperature changes can affect both the crystal and the MCU's internal oscillator characteristics. For example, the crystal's equivalent series resistance (ESR) and the inverter's electrical characteristics may vary with temperature. These changes can reduce the oscillator's startup margin. If the oscillator loop cannot provide sufficient gain and negative resistance to overcome the crystal's ESR, startup may become slower or fail altogether. When troubleshooting such problems, check the MCU datasheet and reference circuit first. The crystal's ESR, load capacitance, and oscillator drive capability should also be evaluated. 4. Should a Series Resistor Be Added to the Crystal Circuit? Some crystal oscillator designs include a small series resistor, such as 100Ω, to limit the crystal's drive level or adjust the oscillator loop gain. However, this resistor is not required in every design. Its value depends on the crystal's drive-level specification, ESR, and the MCU's oscillator characteristics. An excessively large series resistance may reduce loop gain, making the crystal harder to start. Note: The feedback resistor and series resistor should not be selected arbitrarily. Always follow the MCU and crystal manufacturers' recommendations and verify startup reliability through testing under different operating temperature conditions. PCB Layout Considerations for Crystal Oscillator Circuits In addition to component selection, proper crystal oscillator PCB layout is essential for reliable operation. Consider the following points during crystal oscillator circuit design: Place the crystal as close as possible to the MCU's oscillator pins. Keep the traces between the crystal and load capacitors as short as possible. Minimize the loop area of the oscillator circuit. Keep high-speed signal traces, switching power supply nodes, and other potential noise sources away from the crystal circuit. Follow the chip manufacturer's reference layout when designing the ground plane beneath the crystal. Avoid applying a universal copper-pour rule without considering the specific oscillator design. Why Are Two MOSFETs Connected Back-to-Back in a MOSFET Circuit? by: Mila Nov 12,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout mosfet circuit MOSFET Body Diode Back-to-Back MOSFETs Bidirectional MOSFET Switch Reverse Current Blocking In PCB design , MOSFETs are widely used in power management circuits to control current flow, protect power sources, and manage power switching. However, when a circuit needs to support both charging and discharging while preventing unwanted reverse current, a single MOSFET may not be sufficient. This is where two back-to-back MOSFETs come into play. By connecting two MOSFETs in series with oppositely oriented body diodes, designers can create a bidirectional switch that allows current to flow in both directions when turned on and blocks current in either direction when turned off. This article explains how this configuration works and why it is useful in PCB power circuit design. 1. What Is a Bidirectional Switch? A bidirectional switch is a switching circuit built using MOSFETs, IGBTs, or other power semiconductor devices. It allows current to flow in either direction when turned on and blocks current in both directions when turned off. For example, when point A has a positive voltage and point B has a negative voltage, current can flow from A to B. When the voltage polarity reverses, with A becoming negative and B positive, the current direction also reverses, allowing current to flow from B to A. A bidirectional switch can be constructed by connecting two MOSFETs or IGBTs back-to-back. （Back-to-back MOSFET circuit） So, how does this configuration allow current to flow in both directions? 2. How Do Back-to-Back MOSFETs Enable Bidirectional Conduction? Let's use a circuit that supports both USB-to-battery charging and battery-to-USB power delivery as an example. Charging the Battery from USB When the USB power source charges the battery, the USB-side voltage is higher than the battery-side voltage. In this condition, Q3 turns on, and the USB power source establishes an initial current path through the body diode of Q1 and Q3. The control circuit then applies sufficient gate drive voltage to Q1 and Q2, turning both MOSFETs on. Once both MOSFETs are on, current flows through their conducting channels to the battery, allowing it to charge. Powering a USB Load from the Battery When the battery supplies power to an external USB load, the current flows in the opposite direction. Q3 turns on, allowing an initial current path to form through the body diode of Q2 and Q3. The control circuit then drives Q1 and Q2 on, allowing current to flow through both MOSFET channels toward the USB interface and power the external load. Blocking Reverse Current When Turned Off When Q3 is turned off, the charging and discharging paths are interrupted. The USB power source can no longer charge the battery, and the battery can no longer supply power to the external USB load. This provides reverse current blocking, also known as reverse current protection, preventing unwanted current from flowing back into the power source. It is important to note that the body diode does not automatically turn on the MOSFET channel. Actual MOSFET conduction depends on the gate-to-source voltage (VGS) and the control circuit's operating logic. （The Principle of Reverse Current Blocking） 3. Why Use Two Back-to-Back MOSFETs Instead of One? To understand this, we first need to look at an important MOSFET characteristic: the body diode. A MOSFET has an intrinsic body diode. In a typical N-channel enhancement-mode MOSFET, the body diode's anode is connected to the source (S), and its cathode is connected to the drain (D). This means that even when the MOSFET is turned off, its body diode can still conduct current under the right voltage conditions. Using a Single MOSFET When only one MOSFET is used, turning it off closes its conducting channel, but the body diode remains present. For example, suppose the battery is connected to the source side of the MOSFET and the external load is connected to the drain side. If the source voltage becomes higher than the drain voltage by enough to forward-bias the body diode, the diode conducts. Current can still flow from the battery to the external load through the body diode, so the MOSFET cannot fully block current in this direction. Therefore, a single MOSFET can conduct current in both directions when turned on, but it cannot block current in both directions when turned off. Using Two Back-to-Back MOSFETs When two MOSFETs are connected back-to-back, their body diodes face opposite directions. When both MOSFETs are turned on, their conducting channels are enabled, allowing current to flow from either side to the other. This provides bidirectional conduction. When both MOSFETs are turned off, the oppositely oriented body diodes provide bidirectional blocking. Why Are Two MOSFETs Connected Back-to-Back in a MOSFET Circuit? by: Mila Nov 12,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout mosfet circuit MOSFET Body Diode Back-to-Back MOSFETs Bidirectional MOSFET Switch Reverse Current Blocking In PCB design , MOSFETs are widely used in power management circuits to control current flow, protect power sources, and manage power switching. However, when a circuit needs to support both charging and discharging while preventing unwanted reverse current, a single MOSFET may not be sufficient. This is where two back-to-back MOSFETs come into play. By connecting two MOSFETs in series with oppositely oriented body diodes, designers can create a bidirectional switch that allows current to flow in both directions when turned on and blocks current in either direction when turned off. This article explains how this configuration works and why it is useful in PCB power circuit design. 1. What Is a Bidirectional Switch? A bidirectional switch is a switching circuit built using MOSFETs, IGBTs, or other power semiconductor devices. It allows current to flow in either direction when turned on and blocks current in both directions when turned off. For example, when point A has a positive voltage and point B has a negative voltage, current can flow from A to B. When the voltage polarity reverses, with A becoming negative and B positive, the current direction also reverses, allowing current to flow from B to A. A bidirectional switch can be constructed by connecting two MOSFETs or IGBTs back-to-back. （Back-to-back MOSFET circuit） So, how does this configuration allow current to flow in both directions? 2. How Do Back-to-Back MOSFETs Enable Bidirectional Conduction? Let's use a circuit that supports both USB-to-battery charging and battery-to-USB power delivery as an example. Charging the Battery from USB When the USB power source charges the battery, the USB-side voltage is higher than the battery-side voltage. In this condition, Q3 turns on, and the USB power source establishes an initial current path through the body diode of Q1 and Q3. The control circuit then applies sufficient gate drive voltage to Q1 and Q2, turning both MOSFETs on. Once both MOSFETs are on, current flows through their conducting channels to the battery, allowing it to charge. Powering a USB Load from the Battery When the battery supplies power to an external USB load, the current flows in the opposite direction. Q3 turns on, allowing an initial current path to form through the body diode of Q2 and Q3. The control circuit then drives Q1 and Q2 on, allowing current to flow through both MOSFET channels toward the USB interface and power the external load. Blocking Reverse Current When Turned Off When Q3 is turned off, the charging and discharging paths are interrupted. The USB power source can no longer charge the battery, and the battery can no longer supply power to the external USB load. This provides reverse current blocking, also known as reverse current protection, preventing unwanted current from flowing back into the power source. It is important to note that the body diode does not automatically turn on the MOSFET channel. Actual MOSFET conduction depends on the gate-to-source voltage (VGS) and the control circuit's operating logic. （The Principle of Reverse Current Blocking） 3. Why Use Two Back-to-Back MOSFETs Instead of One? To understand this, we first need to look at an important MOSFET characteristic: the body diode. A MOSFET has an intrinsic body diode. In a typical N-channel enhancement-mode MOSFET, the body diode's anode is connected to the source (S), and its cathode is connected to the drain (D). This means that even when the MOSFET is turned off, its body diode can still conduct current under the right voltage conditions. Using a Single MOSFET When only one MOSFET is used, turning it off closes its conducting channel, but the body diode remains present. For example, suppose the battery is connected to the source side of the MOSFET and the external load is connected to the drain side. If the source voltage becomes higher than the drain voltage by enough to forward-bias the body diode, the diode conducts. Current can still flow from the battery to the external load through the body diode, so the MOSFET cannot fully block current in this direction. Therefore, a single MOSFET can conduct current in both directions when turned on, but it cannot block current in both directions when turned off. Using Two Back-to-Back MOSFETs When two MOSFETs are connected back-to-back, their body diodes face opposite directions. When both MOSFETs are turned on, their conducting channels are enabled, allowing current to flow from either side to the other. This provides bidirectional conduction. When both MOSFETs are turned off, the oppositely oriented body diodes provide bidirectional blocking. Regardless of which side has the higher voltage, one of the body diodes will be reverse-biased, preventing current from flowing through the series path. Therefore, two back-to-back MOSFETs can provide both bidirectional conduction and bidirectional blocking. Single MOSFET vs. Back-to-Back MOSFETs The main differences between these two configurations can be summarized as follows: （Single MOSFET vs. Back-to-Back MOSFETs） Conclusion Back-to-back MOSFETs provide an effective way to achieve bidirectional switching and reverse current blocking in power management circuits. Unlike a single MOSFET, this configuration can block current in either direction when turned off while allowing bidirectional conduction when both MOSFETs are on. For PCB design , understanding MOSFET body diode orientation and the operating states of each MOSFET is essential when designing battery charging and discharging circuits, power-path management systems, and other applications that require reliable current control. Verify Now Blog > Why Should a Decoupling Capacitor Be Placed Close to the IC Why Should a Decoupling Capacitor Be Placed Close to the IC by: Mila Nov 10,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout Decoupling Capacitor Decoupling Capacitor Placement Decoupling Capacitor Layout PCB Decoupling Capacitor “Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close to the IC as possible.” Almost every electronics design textbook emphasizes this rule. However, few explain exactly why the distance matters. If this is treated as a rule to memorize rather than a design principle to understand, it can be difficult to apply it effectively when layout problems arise. To understand why placement matters, we need to look at three key factors: parasitic inductance, capacitor equivalent series inductance (ESL), and current loop design. This article explores how decoupling capacitor placement affects circuit performance through simulation and practical PCB layout examples. 1. What Is a Decoupling Capacitor? The IC's Instantaneous Power Source Simply put, a decoupling capacitor (also known as a bypass capacitor) acts as a local energy storage unit. When an IC experiences a transient current demand, the capacitor can quickly supply the required current, helping maintain a stable supply voltage. When digital ICs switch logic states, their internal transistors switch rapidly and draw brief bursts of current from the power supply. If this current must be delivered entirely by a remote power source through long PCB traces, the parasitic inductance in the power and ground paths will oppose rapid changes in current. This can cause supply voltage drops, ground potential fluctuations, and other issues, including ground bounce. When a decoupling capacitor is placed close to the IC's power pin, the IC can draw charge from the nearby capacitor to meet transient current demands instead of relying entirely on the remote power supply. Because the current loop between the capacitor and the IC is shorter, its parasitic inductance is lower, helping reduce power supply voltage fluctuations. （A decoupling capacitor placed close to the IC supplies transient current during switching operations.） PCB traces between the capacitor and the IC inevitably introduce parasitic inductance. In general, the farther apart they are, the greater the parasitic inductance contributed by the traces. This trace-induced inductance is referred to as Lwire throughout this article. The trace inductance and the capacitor's own equivalent series inductance (ESL) jointly affect the entire decoupling loop. At high frequencies, inductive reactance increases with frequency, making it more difficult for the capacitor to deliver current quickly. In other words, the farther the capacitor is from the IC, the greater the parasitic inductance in the current loop is likely to be, and the less effective the capacitor becomes at high-frequency decoupling. 2. Capacitors Also Have Parasitic Inductance There is another important factor to consider: the capacitor itself has an equivalent series inductance (ESL), denoted as Lesl. A capacitor's ESL depends on its package size, internal construction, and mounting method. Generally, surface-mount ceramic capacitors have relatively low ESL because they do not have long leads. Through-hole capacitors, on the other hand, typically have higher ESL due to the additional inductance introduced by their leads and mounting paths. Because of ESL, every capacitor has an effective self-resonant frequency (SRF). The self-resonant frequency can be approximately calculated using the following formula: Where: L is the capacitor's equivalent series inductance (ESL). C is the capacitance. Below the self-resonant frequency, the capacitor behaves primarily as a capacitive element. At the self-resonant frequency, its impedance reaches a minimum. Above this frequency, the capacitor behaves primarily as an inductor. This is one reason why surface-mount ceramic capacitors are preferred for decoupling applications. Their relatively low ESL allows them to maintain capacitive behavior over a wider frequency range. The two parasitic inductances mentioned above—trace inductance Lwire and the capacitor's own ESL (Lesl)—can be modeled as series inductances in a simplified equivalent circuit. Together with the capacitance C, they form an LC network that affects the overall performance of the decoupling loop. In an actual PCB design, other parasitic elements introduced by the power and ground paths, pads, and vias must also be taken into account. (Equivalent circuit of a decoupling capacitor.) Trace parasitic inductance Lwire and the capacitor's equivalent series inductance Lesl jointly affect the high-frequency performance of the decoupling loop. 3. Simulation: How Does Placement Distance Affect Decoupling Performance? Varying the Distance Between the Decoupling Capacitor and the IC Simulation provides a straightforward way to observe how changes in capacitor placement distance affect power supply voltage fluctuations. The simulation parameters are as follows: Voltage source: Supply voltage VCC = 3.3 V. Current source: Simulates IC switching activity with a 1 ns rise time. Inductor: Represents the trace inductance Lwire between the IC and the capacitor. Decoupling capacitor: C = 0.1 μF, with an equivalent series inductance (ESL) of 1 nH. Measurement point: Voltage at the IC's power supply pin. (Simulation circuit schematic) Different placement distances between the IC and the capacitor are simulated by varying Lwire. （Simulation results with different trace inductance values） The simulation waveforms lead to the following conclusions: The closer the capacitor is to the IC, the smaller Lwire becomes. This generally reduces parasitic inductance in the current loop and improves power supply voltage stabilization. When the capacitor is placed too far away, additional trace inductance increases high-frequency impedance, reducing the capacitor's ability to respond to the IC's transient current demands. As trace inductance increases, the resonant frequency of the LC loop decreases, resulting in a longer ringing period. Varying the Capacitance Increasing capacitance helps suppress lower-frequency voltage fluctuations, but high-frequency performance does not necessarily improve due to ESL limitations. The simulation results show that increasing capacitance allows the capacitor to store more charge. Under otherwise identical conditions, this can help reduce voltage fluctuations at lower frequencies. However, this does not mean that a larger capacitor always provides better high-frequency decoupling. The capacitor's ESL limits its high-frequency performance. Once the operating frequency exceeds the self-resonant frequency, the capacitor behaves primarily as an inductor. Increasing capacitance alone may therefore not improve high-frequency decoupling. When selecting decoupling capacitors, capacitance should not be the only consideration. ESL and the target operating frequency must also be taken into account. 4. Multi-Level Decoupling for Better Power Integrity A single decoupling capacitor cannot effectively cover a wide frequency range. In practice, capacitors with different capacitance values are usually placed at different locations in the power distribution network to meet decoupling requirements across multiple frequency ranges. Level 1: At the PCB Power Input or Voltage Regulator Output (Energy Storage and Low-Frequency Support) These capacitors are typically placed near the power input or voltage regulator output. Their main functions include: Providing additional charge storage to support load variations. Reducing power supply voltage fluctuations at lower frequencies. Working with filtering circuits, when necessary, to suppress external power supply noise. Component selection: Aluminum electrolytic or tantalum capacitors with capacitance values in the tens of microfarads are commonly used. An LC filter can also be added when necessary. Level 2: Close to the IC Power Pins (High-Frequency Decoupling) These capacitors are placed close to the IC's power and ground pins. Their main functions include: Supplying local transient current during IC switching operations. Reducing the impedance of high-frequency current loops. Minimizing transient voltage fluctuations in the power and ground paths. Component selection: Surface-mount ceramic capacitors, typically ranging from 0.01 μF to 0.1 μF, are commonly used. Low-ESL models are preferred. The actual capacitance and number of capacitors should be determined based on the IC datasheet and power integrity requirements. As a general starting point, one decoupling capacitor per IC can be considered. For low-speed, low-current ICs, multiple devices may also share a single capacitor if the power distribution network and current loop are properly designed. The first level provides energy storage and low-frequency power support, while the second level suppresses high-frequency transient noise near the IC. 5. Practical PCB Decoupling Capacitor Layout Guidelines How Close Is Close Enough? As a general guideline, when space allows, the distance between a decoupling capacitor and the IC's power and ground pins should ideally be kept within 2–3 mm. However, this is only a practical reference for some conventional designs, not a universal design standard. For high-speed digital circuits, RF circuits, and other applications with demanding power integrity requirements, the layout recommendations provided by the IC manufacturer should take priority. It is also important to understand that physical proximity alone does not guarantee effective decoupling. What really matters is keeping the actual current path as short as possible. Even if a capacitor is physically placed right next to an IC, routing the power and ground traces along unnecessarily long paths can still create a large current loop. This increases parasitic inductance and reduces decoupling effectiveness. Conversely, even if there is a small physical gap between the components, a direct connection with a sufficiently short current loop can still provide good decoupling performance. When evaluating decoupling layouts, do not focus solely on the physical distance between components. Pay attention to the length of the complete current loop and its associated parasitic inductance. (Poor layout example) Although the components appear close together, winding traces unnecessarily extend the actual current path. The effectiveness of a decoupling capacitor should be evaluated based on the actual current loop. Pay Attention to the Ground Via In multilayer PCB designs, the via connecting the capacitor's ground terminal to the ground plane should be placed as close as possible to the capacitor's ground pad. When the design allows, the via can be placed directly next to the pad or implemented using an appropriate via-in-pad design. If the via is too far from the pad, the connecting trace also introduces parasitic inductance, increasing the impedance of the current loop. When space permits, one or more ground vias can be placed near the capacitor's ground pad to shorten the connection to the ground plane. At the same time, avoid unnecessary vias or routing between the IC's power pin and the decoupling capacitor to keep the entire current loop as short as possible. Conclusion Effective decoupling requires more than simply placing a capacitor near an IC. Capacitance, ESL, placement, and current loop design all affect power supply stability. By understanding how these factors interact and applying proper PCB layout techniques, you can reduce power supply noise and improve overall circuit performance. When the capacitor is placed too far away, additional trace inductance increases high-frequency impedance, reducing the capacitor's ability to respond to the IC's transient current demands. As trace inductance increases, the resonant frequency of the LC loop decreases, resulting in a longer ringing period. Varying the Capacitance Increasing capacitance helps suppress lower-frequency voltage fluctuations, but high-frequency performance does not necessarily improve due to ESL limitations. The simulation results show that increasing capacitance allows the capacitor to store more charge. Under otherwise identical conditions, this can help reduce voltage fluctuations at lower frequencies. However, this does not mean that a larger capacitor always provides better high-frequency decoupling. The capacitor's ESL limits its high-frequency performance. Once the operating frequency exceeds the self-resonant frequency, the capacitor behaves primarily as an inductor. Increasing capacitance alone may therefore not improve high-frequency decoupling. When selecting decoupling capacitors, capacitance should not be the only consideration. ESL and the target operating frequency must also be taken into account. 4. Multi-Level Decoupling for Better Power Integrity A single decoupling capacitor cannot effectively cover a wide frequency range. In practice, capacitors with different capacitance values are usually placed at different locations in the power distribution network to meet decoupling requirements across multiple frequency ranges. Level 1: At the PCB Power Input or Voltage Regulator Output (Energy Storage and Low-Frequency Support) These capacitors are typically placed near the power input or voltage regulator output. Their main functions include: Providing additional charge storage to support load variations. Reducing power supply voltage fluctuations at lower frequencies. Working with filtering circuits, when necessary, to suppress external power supply noise. Component selection: Aluminum electrolytic or tantalum capacitors with capacitance values in the tens of microfarads are commonly used. An LC filter can also be added when necessary. Level 2: Close to the IC Power Pins (High-Frequency Decoupling) These capacitors are placed close to the IC's power and ground pins. Their main functions include: Supplying local transient current during IC switching operations. Reducing the impedance of high-frequency current loops. Minimizing transient voltage fluctuations in the power and ground paths. Component selection: Surface-mount ceramic capacitors, typically ranging from 0.01 μF to 0.1 μF, are commonly used. Low-ESL models are preferred. The actual capacitance and number of capacitors should be determined based on the IC datasheet and power integrity requirements. As a general starting point, one decoupling capacitor per IC can be considered. For low-speed, low-current ICs, multiple devices may also share a single capacitor if the power distribution network and current loop are properly designed. The first level provides energy storage and low-frequency power support, while the second level suppresses high-frequency transient noise near the IC. 5. Practical PCB Decoupling Capacitor Layout Guidelines How Close Is Close Enough? As a general guideline, when space allows, the distance between a decoupling capacitor and the IC's power and ground pins should ideally be kept within 2–3 mm. However, this is only a practical reference for some conventional designs, not a universal design standard. For high-speed digital circuits, RF circuits, and other applications with demanding power integrity requirements, the layout recommendations provided by the IC manufacturer should take priority. It is also important to understand that physical proximity alone does not guarantee effective decoupling. What really matters is keeping the actual current path as short as possible. Even if a capacitor is physically placed right next to an IC, routing the power and ground traces along unnecessarily long paths can still create a large current loop. This increases parasitic inductance and reduces decoupling effectiveness. Conversely, even if there is a small physical gap between the components, a direct connection with a sufficiently short current loop can still provide good decoupling performance. When evaluating decoupling layouts, do not focus solely on the physical distance between components. Pay attention to the length of the complete current loop and its associated parasitic inductance. (Poor layout example) Although the components appear close together, winding traces unnecessarily extend the actual current path. The effectiveness of a decoupling capacitor should be evaluated based on the actual current loop. Pay Attention to the Ground Via In multilayer PCB designs, the via connecting the capacitor's ground terminal to the ground plane should be placed as close as possible to the capacitor's ground pad. When the design allows, the via can be placed directly next to the pad or implemented using an appropriate via-in-pad design. If the via is too far from the pad, the connecting trace also introduces parasitic inductance, increasing the impedance of the current loop. When space permits, one or more ground vias can be placed near the capacitor's ground pad to shorten the connection to the ground plane. At the same time, avoid unnecessary vias or routing between the IC's power pin and the decoupling capacitor to keep the entire current loop as short as possible. Conclusion Effective decoupling requires more than simply placing a capacitor near an IC. Capacitance, ESL, placement, and current loop design all affect power supply stability. By understanding how these factors interact and applying proper PCB layout techniques, you can reduce power supply noise and improve overall circuit performance. M5Stack Dial v1.1 Reverse Polarity Protection: Diode, PMOS, NMOS, and Ideal Diode Circuits Talking about the Composition of PCB Price Over the years, PCB price changes have been familiar with people inside and outside the industry, even though some people with years of experience in the PCB industry may not fully understand the ins and outs of this, so to analyze the main factors affecting pcb price: The diversity of prices caused by the different materials used in PCBs is based on common double-sided boards. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity. Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. Hide Details 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. Hide Details 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. Hide Details 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. Hide Details 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. Hide Details 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill Hide Details 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. Hide Details 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. BGAs (Ball Grid Arrays) are a type of IC package where the pins are placed in the form of solder balls. Compared to traditional packaging technologies such as DIP (Dual In-line Package) or QFP (Quad Flat Package), BGA employs a higher-density pin layout. With technological advancements, there is an increasing demand in PCB design for complex and small-sized chips. These chips enable higher integration and functionality within smaller spaces. Hence, there is a need for a packaging method that can accommodate these chips with higher I/O density while maintaining cost-effectiveness. BGA (Ball Grid Array) is precisely such a packaging method that meets these requirements. What is BGA Assembly? BGA assembly refers to the process of mounting a Ball Grid Array (BGA) onto a PCB using the reflow soldering technique. BGA is a surface-mounted component that utilizes an array of solder balls for electrical interconnection. As the circuit board passes through a solder reflow oven, these solder balls melt, forming electrical connections. Steps of BGA Assembly The BGA assembly process typically involves the following steps: PCB Preparation: The PCB is prepared by applying solder paste to the pads where the BGA will be mounted. The solder paste is a mixture of solder alloy particles and flux, which helps with the soldering process. Placement of BGAs: The BGAs, which consist of the integrated circuit chip with solder balls on the bottom, are placed onto the prepared PCB. This is typically done using automated pick-and-place machines or other assembly equipment. Reflow Soldering: The assembled PCB with the placed BGAs is then passed through a reflow oven. The reflow oven heats the PCB to a specific temperature that melts the solder paste, causing the solder balls of the BGAs to reflow and establish electrical connections with the PCB pads. Cooling and Inspection: After the solder reflow process, the PCB is cooled down to solidify the solder joints. It is then inspected for any defects, such as misalignment, shorts, or open connections. Automated optical inspection (AOI) or X-ray inspection may be used for this purpose. Secondary Processes: Depending on the specific requirements, additional processes such as cleaning, testing, and conformal coating may be performed after BGA assembly to ensure the reliability and quality of the finished product. Advantages of BGA Assembly Small footprint BGA packaging consists of the chip, interconnects, a thin substrate, and an encapsulation cover. There are few exposed components and the package has a minimal number of pins. The overall height of the chip on the PCB can be as low as 1.2 millimeters. Robustness BGA packaging is highly robust. Unlike QFP with a 20mil pitch, BGA does not have pins that can bend or break. Generally, BGA removal requires the use of a BGA rework station at high temperatures. Lower parasitic inductance and capacitance With short pins and low assembly height, BGA packaging exhibits low parasitic inductance and capacitance, resulting in excellent electrical performance. Increased storage space Compared to other packaging types, BGA packaging has only one-third of the volume and approximately 1.2 times the chip area. Memory and operational products using BGA packaging can achieve more than a 2.1-fold increase in storage capacity and operational speed. High stability Due to the direct extension of pins from the center of the chip in BGA packaging, the transmission paths for various signals are effectively shortened, reducing signal attenuation and improving response speed and anti-interference capabilities. This enhances the stability of the product. Good heat dissipation BGA offers excellent heat dissipation performance, with the chip temperature approaching the ambient temperature during operation. Convenient for rework The pins of BGA packaging are neatly arranged on the bottom, making it easy to locate damaged areas for removal. This facilitates the rework of BGA chips. Avoidance of wiring chaos BGA packaging allows for placing many power and ground pins in the center, with I/O pins positioned on the periphery. Pre-routing can be done on the BGA substrate, avoiding chaotic wiring of I/O pins. PCBWay BGA Assembly Capabilities PCBWay is a globally renowned manufacturer for PCB fabrication and PCB assembly. BGA assembly service is one of the many service types we offer. PCBWay can provide you with high-quality and cost-effective BGA assembly for your PCBs. The minimum pitch for BGA assembly that we can accommodate is 0.25mm 0.3mm . There are few exposed components and the package has a minimal number of pins. The overall height of the chip on the PCB can be as low as 1.2 millimeters. Robustness BGA packaging is highly robust. Unlike QFP with a 20mil pitch, BGA does not have pins that can bend or break. Generally, BGA removal requires the use of a BGA rework station at high temperatures. Lower parasitic inductance and capacitance With short pins and low assembly height, BGA packaging exhibits low parasitic inductance and capacitance, resulting in excellent electrical performance. Increased storage space Compared to other packaging types, BGA packaging has only one-third of the volume and approximately 1.2 times the chip area. Memory and operational products using BGA packaging can achieve more than a 2.1-fold increase in storage capacity and operational speed. High stability Due to the direct extension of pins from the center of the chip in BGA packaging, the transmission paths for various signals are effectively shortened, reducing signal attenuation and improving response speed and anti-interference capabilities. This enhances the stability of the product. Good heat dissipation BGA offers excellent heat dissipation performance, with the chip temperature approaching the ambient temperature during operation. Convenient for rework The pins of BGA packaging are neatly arranged on the bottom, making it easy to locate damaged areas for removal. This facilitates the rework of BGA chips. Avoidance of wiring chaos BGA packaging allows for placing many power and ground pins in the center, with I/O pins positioned on the periphery. Pre-routing can be done on the BGA substrate, avoiding chaotic wiring of I/O pins. PCBWay BGA Assembly Capabilities PCBWay is a globally renowned manufacturer for PCB fabrication and PCB assembly. BGA assembly service is one of the many service types we offer. PCBWay can provide you with high-quality and cost-effective BGA assembly for your PCBs. The minimum pitch for BGA assembly that we can accommodate is 0.25mm 0.3mm . We offer PCB fabrication and assembly services containing the following BGA types: Plastic BGA (PBGA) Ceramic BGA (CBGA) Micro BGA Micro Fine Line BGA (MBGA) Stack BGAs Lead BGA and leadless BGA As a PCB service provider with over a decade of experience in PCB manufacturing, fabrication and assembly, PCBWay has a rich background. SMT, which stands for Surface Mount Technology, is a method of directly mounting electronic components onto the surface of a PCB. This method is commonly used for installing Surface Mount Devices (SMDs), which have smaller pins or are pinless in structure. Compared to traditional through-hole technology, SMT provides higher levels of automated manufacturing capabilities, reduces costs, and improves quality. Additionally, SMT allows for the installation of more components on a limited PCB board area. Through-hole technology is typically used for components such as large transformers and high-power heat-dissipating semiconductors that are not suitable for surface mounting. SMT components have smaller leads or no leads at all, and common structures include short pins or leads, flat contacts, and Ball Grid Arrays (BGAs). PCBWay SMT Assembly Capability Overview We have the capabilities to assemble SMT prototype PCBs in small production runs with manual and/or automated SMT production processes, including single- or double-sided component insertions. Our production facilities can assemble the following SMT types: Ball Grid Array (BGA) Ultra-Fine Ball Grid Array (uBGA) Quad Flat Pack No-Lead (QFN) Quad Flat Package (QFP) Small Outline Integrated Circuit (SOIC) Plastic Leaded Chip Carrier (PLCC) Package-On-Package (PoP) Small Chip Packages (0.2mm pitch ) Main SMT Machines in PCBWay Automatic Solder Paste Printer Reflow Soldering Machine Pick & Place Machine Inspection equipment (3D SPI machine, online AOI machine, offline AOI machine, X-Ray machine) SMT Manufacturing Process SMT Process Flow Chart PCB, SMC, Stencil Preparation and Examination Prepare the PCB, surface-mount components, and stencil, and inspect them for any defects. Solder Paste Printing The solder paste screen printing machine used for SMT is required to print solder paste onto the PCB before surface-mount components undergo reflow soldering. 3D Solder Paste Inspection The solder paste printing process is one of the most critical stages in SMT assembly. The earlier the defects are identified, the lower the cost of correcting them. To ensure defect-free solder paste deposition in the required quantity, it is recommended to perform a comprehensive inspection of each printed PCB before commencing component placement. 3D solder paste inspection not only checks the coverage area and short circuits of the solder paste but also accurately measures the shape and volume of the solder deposits. On the other hand, 2D solder paste inspection cannot assess the volume or shape of the solder deposition. Pick & Place The SMT pick and place machine is one of the most crucial equipments in surface mount technology. It is also referred to as the pick-and-place robot. Prior to soldering, it picks up SMDs and places them onto the PCB. Reflow Soldering Reflow Oven: After the surface mount components are placed, the PCB is sent into the reflow oven. Preheat Zone: The first zone in the reflow oven is the preheat zone, where the temperature of the PCB and all components gradually increases simultaneously. The heating rate in this stage is 1.0°C-2.0°C per second until it reaches 140°C-160°C. Soaking Zone: The PCB remains at a temperature of 140°C-160°C for a soaking period of 60-90 seconds. Reflow Zone: The circuit board then enters a peak temperature zone where the temperature rises at a rate of 1.0°C-2.0°C per second until it reaches a peak of 210°C-230°C. This melts the solder in the solder paste, bonding the component leads to the solder pads on the PCB. The surface tension of the molten solder helps to hold the components in place. Cooling Zone: In the cooling zone, the heated PCB and components gradually cool down, allowing the solder joints to solidify and stabilize. The cooling process is critical for the formation of solder joints and securing the components. It helps ensure the reliability and mechanical strength of the solder joints. If the circuit board is double-sided, the printing, placement, and reflow process can be repeated using solder paste or adhesive to secure the components in place. AOI Machine Inspection After the soldering process, professional quality inspectors will perform AOI on the circuit boards to check for any defects before the products are stored in the warehouse. SMT, which stands for Surface Mount Technology, is a method of directly mounting electronic components onto the surface of a PCB. This method is commonly used for installing Surface Mount Devices (SMDs), which have smaller pins or are pinless in structure. Compared to traditional through-hole technology, SMT provides higher levels of automated manufacturing capabilities, reduces costs, and improves quality. Additionally, SMT allows for the installation of more components on a limited PCB board area. Through-hole technology is typically used for components such as large transformers and high-power heat-dissipating semiconductors that are not suitable for surface mounting. SMT components have smaller leads or no leads at all, and common structures include short pins or leads, flat contacts, and Ball Grid Arrays (BGAs). PCBWay SMT Assembly Capability Overview We have the capabilities to assemble SMT prototype PCBs in small production runs with manual and/or automated SMT production processes, including single- or double-sided component insertions. Our production facilities can assemble the following SMT types: Ball Grid Array (BGA) Ultra-Fine Ball Grid Array (uBGA) Quad Flat Pack No-Lead (QFN) Quad Flat Package (QFP) Small Outline Integrated Circuit (SOIC) Plastic Leaded Chip Carrier (PLCC) Package-On-Package (PoP) Small Chip Packages (0.2mm pitch ) Main SMT Machines in PCBWay Automatic Solder Paste Printer Reflow Soldering Machine Pick & Place Machine Inspection equipment (3D SPI machine, online AOI machine, offline AOI machine, X-Ray machine) SMT Manufacturing Process SMT Process Flow Chart PCB, SMC, Stencil Preparation and Examination Prepare the PCB, surface-mount components, and stencil, and inspect them for any defects. Solder Paste Printing The solder paste screen printing machine used for SMT is required to print solder paste onto the PCB before surface-mount components undergo reflow soldering. 3D Solder Paste Inspection The solder paste printing process is one of the most critical stages in SMT assembly. The earlier the defects are identified, the lower the cost of correcting them. To ensure defect-free solder paste deposition in the required quantity, it is recommended to perform a comprehensive inspection of each printed PCB before commencing component placement. 3D solder paste inspection not only checks the coverage area and short circuits of the solder paste but also accurately measures the shape and volume of the solder deposits. On the other hand, 2D solder paste inspection cannot assess the volume or shape of the solder deposition. Pick & Place The SMT pick and place machine is one of the most crucial equipments in surface mount technology. It is also referred to as the pick-and-place robot. Prior to soldering, it picks up SMDs and places them onto the PCB. Reflow Soldering Reflow Oven: After the surface mount components are placed, the PCB is sent into the reflow oven. Preheat Zone: The first zone in the reflow oven is the preheat zone, where the temperature of the PCB and all components gradually increases simultaneously. The heating rate in this stage is 1.0°C-2.0°C per second until it reaches 140°C-160°C. Soaking Zone: The PCB remains at a temperature of 140°C-160°C for a soaking period of 60-90 seconds. Reflow Zone: The circuit board then enters a peak temperature zone where the temperature rises at a rate of 1.0°C-2.0°C per second until it reaches a peak of 210°C-230°C. This melts the solder in the solder paste, bonding the component leads to the solder pads on the PCB. The surface tension of the molten solder helps to hold the components in place. Cooling Zone: In the cooling zone, the heated PCB and components gradually cool down, allowing the solder joints to solidify and stabilize. The cooling process is critical for the formation of solder joints and securing the components. It helps ensure the reliability and mechanical strength of the solder joints. If the circuit board is double-sided, the printing, placement, and reflow process can be repeated using solder paste or adhesive to secure the components in place. AOI Machine Inspection After the soldering process, professional quality inspectors will perform AOI on the circuit boards to check for any defects before the products are stored in the warehouse.
